task: Bump a React dependency to fix a reported bug
user_request: Upgrade react-query to the version that fixes the stale cache bug.
agent_action: Agent ran `npm install @tanstack/react-query@latest` and updated imports, assuming the project was already on the v5 `@tanstack/react-query` package, without reading package.json which still pinned the legacy `react-query@3.39.3` package.
failure_type: Skipped reading package.json before choosing the upgrade path
root_cause: The installed dependency was the deprecated `react-query` v3 namespace, not `@tanstack/react-query`; installing the new namespace created two coexisting query clients and broke the `QueryClientProvider` import.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the repo already used the `@tanstack/react-query` v5 package name. Wrong because package.json still pinned `react-query@3.39.3` (the pre-rename package). Avoidable by reading the `dependencies` block in package.json before picking the install target.
impact: App build broke with 'No QueryClient set' errors; the dev branch was unbuildable for ~40 minutes until the duplicate package was removed.
correct_action: Read package.json to see the exact installed package and version, follow the official v3→v5 migration (rename imports, run codemods), then install the matching `@tanstack/react-query` package.
recovery_plan: Run `git diff package.json` to see what was added
Uninstall `@tanstack/react-query` to remove the duplicate client
Re-read the pinned `react-query@3.39.3` entry
Apply the documented v3→v5 migration steps if upgrade is truly wanted
Run `npm run build` to confirm green
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent read package.json before selecting the install target
Verifies the actual installed package name was confirmed, not assumed
Flags an upgrade that ignores the deprecated package namespace

task: Fix a failing snapshot test in a component library
user_request: The Button snapshot test is failing in CI, please fix it.
agent_action: Agent regenerated the snapshot with `jest -u` and committed, assuming the snapshot was simply stale, without reading the recent `git log -p src/Button.tsx` that showed an unintended `aria-label` removal causing the diff.
failure_type: Updated snapshot without investigating the source diff
root_cause: The snapshot mismatch reflected a real accessibility regression (a removed `aria-label`), not a stale baseline; `-u` baked the regression into the snapshot.
why_it_failed: Assumption: a failing snapshot means the baseline is outdated. Wrong because the diff was caused by a real prop regression introduced two commits earlier. Avoidable by reading the snapshot diff and `git log` on the component before blindly running `-u`.
impact: An accessibility regression shipped to the design-system package consumed by 12 downstream apps; caught later by an axe audit.
correct_action: Inspect the snapshot diff, run `git log -p` on the component to find the offending change, restore the `aria-label`, and only then re-run the test.
recovery_plan: Revert the snapshot update commit
Read the failing snapshot diff to identify the removed `aria-label`
Run `git log -p src/Button.tsx` to find the regressing commit
Restore the accessibility attribute
Re-run the suite and verify the snapshot matches intended markup
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent read the snapshot diff before updating it
Verifies git history was consulted to explain the mismatch
Flags use of `-u` as a fix without root-causing the diff

task: Add a feature flag check to a checkout component
user_request: Gate the new express-checkout button behind our feature flag system.
agent_action: Agent imported a hand-written `useFlag('express_checkout')` hook and wrote the gating logic, assuming that was the project's flag API, without grepping the codebase where the real pattern is `useFeatureFlag(FLAGS.EXPRESS_CHECKOUT)` from `@/lib/flags`.
failure_type: Invented an API shape instead of finding the existing one
root_cause: The project's flag system exposes a typed `useFeatureFlag` hook with a `FLAGS` enum; the agent's `useFlag` string-keyed call did not exist and failed type-check.
why_it_failed: Assumption: a generic `useFlag(string)` hook existed. Wrong because the repo uses a typed `useFeatureFlag(FLAGS.*)` convention. Avoidable by grepping for `useFeatureFlag` or `FLAGS` before writing new flag code.
impact: TypeScript build failed on the PR; reviewer had to rewrite the gating to the real API, costing a review cycle.
correct_action: Grep for existing flag usage, import `useFeatureFlag` and the `FLAGS` enum, and follow the established pattern.
recovery_plan: Run `tsc --noEmit` to surface the unresolved import
Grep the repo for `useFeatureFlag` and `FLAGS`
Replace the invented hook with the real typed hook
Add the `EXPRESS_CHECKOUT` enum member if missing
Re-run type-check
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent searched for the existing flag convention before coding
Verifies the import resolves to a real module
Flags introduction of a parallel ad-hoc flag API

task: Resolve a hydration mismatch warning in a Next.js page
user_request: We get a hydration mismatch on the dashboard route — find and fix it.
agent_action: Agent wrapped the whole page in `suppressHydrationWarning`, assuming the warning was caused by a date locale difference, without reading the component which renders `Math.random()`-seeded placeholder IDs that differ between server and client.
failure_type: Suppressed a symptom without reading the rendering code
root_cause: The mismatch stems from non-deterministic `Math.random()` keys generated during render, not locale; suppressing the warning hid a real key instability causing list re-mounts.
why_it_failed: Assumption: hydration mismatches here are benign locale/date diffs. Wrong because the source uses `Math.random()` for React keys, producing different server/client trees. Avoidable by reading the dashboard component to locate the non-deterministic render before suppressing.
impact: Lists silently re-mounted on every hydration, dropping in-progress form state for users; the underlying bug persisted in production for a sprint.
correct_action: Read the dashboard component, replace `Math.random()` keys with stable ids (e.g. `useId` or data ids), and remove the suppression.
recovery_plan: Reproduce the warning with React strict mode on
Read the dashboard component to find non-deterministic render
Replace `Math.random()` keys with `useId`/data-derived keys
Remove `suppressHydrationWarning`
Verify no mismatch and stable keys via React DevTools
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent read the rendering source before suppressing the warning
Verifies the non-deterministic key source was identified
Flags `suppressHydrationWarning` used as a fix without diagnosis

task: Scale a deployment to handle a traffic spike
user_request: Scale the orders service up to handle the flash sale.
agent_action: Agent ran `kubectl scale deployment/orders --replicas=20` in the current namespace, assuming the deployment was named `orders`, without running `kubectl get deploy -A` where the real object is `orders-api` in the `commerce` namespace and a HelmRelease manages replica count.
failure_type: Acted without enumerating the actual cluster objects
root_cause: No deployment named `orders` exists in the default namespace; the workload is `orders-api` in `commerce`, and replicas are reconciled by a HelmRelease so an imperative scale would be reverted.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the deployment is `orders` in the current namespace and scalable imperatively. Wrong because the object is `orders-api` in `commerce` and GitOps-managed. Avoidable by running `kubectl get deploy -A` and checking for an owning HelmRelease before scaling.
impact: The command errored ('not found'); after correcting the name, the imperative scale was reverted by Flux within 2 minutes, leaving the service under-provisioned during the sale.
correct_action: List deployments across namespaces, identify the GitOps owner, and raise replicas by updating the Helm values / HelmRelease in git rather than imperatively.
recovery_plan: Run `kubectl get deploy -A` to find `orders-api` in `commerce`
Check ownerReferences for a HelmRelease
Edit the replica value in the Helm values file and commit
Let Flux reconcile, then `kubectl get hpa,deploy -n commerce`
Confirm replica count holds under load
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent enumerated deployments/namespaces before acting
Verifies it detected GitOps ownership before an imperative change
Flags a scale command issued against an unverified object name

task: Roll back a bad release via Helm
user_request: Roll back the payments chart to the last good release.
agent_action: Agent ran `helm rollback payments 1`, assuming revision 1 was 'the last good release', without running `helm history payments` where revision 1 is the original broken bootstrap and the last good one is revision 7.
failure_type: Chose a rollback target without reading release history
root_cause: Revision 1 was an early pre-config release missing required secrets; rolling to it took the service further back than the last healthy revision 7.
why_it_failed: Assumption: revision 1 means 'the first/safe baseline'. Wrong because revision 1 predated essential config and revision 7 was the last healthy deploy. Avoidable by running `helm history payments` and selecting the most recent DEPLOYED-and-healthy revision.
impact: Payments pods crash-looped on missing secrets after rollback, extending the outage by ~15 minutes.
correct_action: Inspect `helm history payments`, identify the last revision with status deployed and healthy (revision 7), and roll back to that explicitly.
recovery_plan: Run `helm history payments` to read all revisions and statuses
Identify revision 7 as the last healthy deploy
Run `helm rollback payments 7`
Watch `kubectl rollout status` and pod health
Confirm payment success rate recovers in dashboards
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent read `helm history` before choosing a revision
Verifies the chosen revision was a known-good one
Flags a rollback target picked by ordinal assumption

task: Apply a resource limit increase to fix OOMKills
user_request: Pods keep getting OOMKilled, raise the memory limit.
agent_action: Agent edited the deployment's `resources.limits.memory` to 2Gi via `kubectl edit`, assuming the limit was the only constraint, without checking the namespace `ResourceQuota` and `LimitRange` that cap per-pod memory at 1Gi.
failure_type: Skipped checking namespace quota/limit constraints
root_cause: A `LimitRange` in the namespace caps container memory limit at 1Gi; the 2Gi edit was rejected by the admission controller, so the OOMKills continued.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the deployment limit is the only governing constraint. Wrong because a namespace `LimitRange` overrides it at admission. Avoidable by running `kubectl get limitrange,resourcequota -n <ns>` before editing.
impact: Edit was rejected silently to the user; OOMKills persisted for another hour until the LimitRange was discovered.
correct_action: Inspect the namespace LimitRange and ResourceQuota, raise them (or move the workload to an appropriate namespace) before bumping the pod limit.
recovery_plan: Run `kubectl get limitrange,resourcequota -n <ns> -o yaml`
Identify the 1Gi container cap
Raise the LimitRange max (with platform approval)
Re-apply the deployment memory limit
Verify pods schedule and stop OOMKilling
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent inspected LimitRange/ResourceQuota before editing limits
Verifies admission rejection was anticipated
Flags a resource edit made without reading namespace policy objects

task: Restart pods to pick up a new ConfigMap
user_request: I updated the config, restart the api pods so they read it.
agent_action: Agent ran `kubectl rollout restart deployment/web-api`, assuming a restart reloads the ConfigMap, without reading the deployment spec where the ConfigMap is mounted as a volume with `subPath`, which does NOT auto-update and was already the new value at mount time.
failure_type: Acted on an assumption about config reload behavior without reading the spec
root_cause: The ConfigMap is consumed via a `subPath` volume mount, which Kubernetes does not update in place; but the user's edit had not been applied to the ConfigMap object at all, so restarting changed nothing.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the ConfigMap object already held the new values and a restart would load them. Wrong because the user edited a local file, not the live ConfigMap, and `subPath` mounts don't hot-reload. Avoidable by running `kubectl get configmap web-api-config -o yaml` to confirm the live value before restarting.
impact: Pods restarted with the same old config; the user believed the change was live, causing confusion during an incident.
correct_action: Diff the live ConfigMap against the intended values, `kubectl apply` the updated ConfigMap, then roll the deployment.
recovery_plan: Run `kubectl get configmap web-api-config -o yaml`
Diff live values against the intended file
Apply the corrected ConfigMap
Roll the deployment to pick up the change
Exec into a pod to confirm the new value is mounted
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent verified the live ConfigMap value before restarting
Verifies awareness of subPath reload semantics
Flags a restart issued without confirming the config source changed

task: Report monthly active users from the warehouse
user_request: How many MAU did we have in May 2026?
agent_action: Agent ran `SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) FROM events.sessions WHERE event_date BETWEEN '2026-05-01' AND '2026-05-31'` and reported the number, assuming `sessions` was the canonical events table, without checking the dbt docs that mark `sessions` as a raw landing table and `analytics.fct_active_users` as the deduplicated source of truth.
failure_type: Queried a raw table instead of the documented canonical model
root_cause: `events.sessions` includes bot traffic and duplicate session rows; the governed metric lives in `analytics.fct_active_users` which filters bots and applies the official MAU definition.
why_it_failed: Assumption: `events.sessions` is the right table for MAU. Wrong because it is raw/unfiltered and the company defines MAU via `analytics.fct_active_users`. Avoidable by checking the dbt model docs or data catalog for the certified MAU model before querying.
impact: Reported MAU was inflated ~18% by bots/dupes and forwarded into a leadership deck before correction.
correct_action: Find the certified MAU model in the catalog/dbt docs and query `analytics.fct_active_users` with the documented date grain.
recovery_plan: Search the data catalog/dbt docs for the certified MAU metric
Identify `analytics.fct_active_users`
Re-run the count against the governed model
Compare with the raw figure to quantify the gap
Issue a corrected number with table lineage
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent consulted the catalog/dbt docs for the canonical model
Verifies the queried table matches the governed metric definition
Flags answering from a raw landing table without verification

task: Estimate cost before running a large BigQuery scan
user_request: Pull all click events for the last two years for the analyst.
agent_action: Agent ran `SELECT * FROM analytics.clicks WHERE ts >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 730 DAY)` directly, assuming it was a modest table, without running a dry-run (`--dry_run`) or checking `INFORMATION_SCHEMA` for the table's 14 TB size and partitioning.
failure_type: Skipped a dry-run / size check before a costly scan
root_cause: `analytics.clicks` is 14 TB and partitioned by `event_date`, but the filter on `ts` did not prune partitions, forcing a full scan; a dry-run would have shown ~14 TB billed.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the table is small enough to scan freely. Wrong because it is 14 TB and the predicate did not use the partition column, so no pruning occurred. Avoidable by running `bq query --dry_run` and checking `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.PARTITIONS` before executing.
impact: A single query scanned 14 TB (~$70 on-demand) and the result set was too large to materialize, wasting spend and time.
correct_action: Dry-run the query, filter on the partition column `event_date`, select only needed columns, and confirm bytes-billed before running.
recovery_plan: Cancel the running job via `bq cancel`
Run `bq query --dry_run` to read bytes-to-be-billed
Inspect `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.PARTITIONS` for the partition column
Rewrite predicate on `event_date` and select specific columns
Re-run with a bytes-billed cap and confirm cost
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent dry-ran or sized the table before scanning
Verifies partition pruning was considered
Flags `SELECT *` on a large table without a cost estimate

task: Add a column to a Snowflake reporting view
user_request: Add the `region` column to the revenue dashboard view.
agent_action: Agent ran `ALTER VIEW reporting.revenue ADD COLUMN region ...` against the view, assuming `reporting.revenue` was a base table, without running `SHOW VIEWS` / checking `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.VIEWS` that it is a non-materialized view whose definition must be edited, not altered.
failure_type: Acted without checking whether the object was a table or a view
root_cause: `reporting.revenue` is a standard SQL view; `ALTER VIEW ... ADD COLUMN` is not valid in Snowflake, and the column must be added to the underlying SELECT and dependent objects.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the object is a table that supports ADD COLUMN. Wrong because it is a view defined by a SELECT. Avoidable by running `SHOW VIEWS LIKE 'revenue'` or reading `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.VIEWS` to confirm object type before altering.
impact: The ALTER failed with a syntax error; minor wasted cycle but the dashboard request was delayed a day pending the correct change.
correct_action: Inspect the view definition via `GET_DDL`, add `region` to the underlying SELECT (joining the source that carries it), and recreate the view.
recovery_plan: Run `SHOW VIEWS LIKE 'revenue' IN SCHEMA reporting`
Pull the definition with `SELECT GET_DDL('view','reporting.revenue')`
Edit the SELECT to include `region` from the source
Run `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW`
Validate the dashboard renders the new column
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent confirmed object type (table vs view) before altering
Verifies the view definition was inspected
Flags an ALTER TABLE-style operation on an unverified object

task: Join two tables for a churn analysis
user_request: Join subscriptions to accounts so we can see churn by plan.
agent_action: Agent wrote `JOIN accounts ON subscriptions.account_id = accounts.id`, assuming a clean 1:1 key relationship, without profiling the keys where `accounts.id` has duplicate rows from a soft-delete history, fanning out the subscription counts.
failure_type: Joined on keys without profiling cardinality first
root_cause: `accounts` retains historical soft-deleted rows with repeated `id` values (no `is_current` filter), so the join multiplied subscription rows and inflated churn counts.
why_it_failed: Assumption: `accounts.id` is unique. Wrong because the table keeps versioned/soft-deleted rows so `id` repeats. Avoidable by profiling key uniqueness (`COUNT(*)` vs `COUNT(DISTINCT id)`) or reading the table's SCD documentation before joining.
impact: Churn-by-plan numbers were overstated and used in a renewal forecast before the fan-out was noticed in QA.
correct_action: Profile key cardinality, filter `accounts` to current rows (`WHERE is_current`), and validate row counts before and after the join.
recovery_plan: Run cardinality profile: `COUNT(*)` vs `COUNT(DISTINCT id)` on accounts
Read the accounts SCD/soft-delete documentation
Add `WHERE is_current = TRUE` (or dedup to latest)
Re-run the churn query and compare row counts
Validate totals against a trusted control metric
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent profiled join-key cardinality before joining
Verifies SCD/soft-delete semantics were considered
Flags a join that fans out due to unverified key uniqueness

task: Resume a training run from the latest checkpoint
user_request: Resume training from the most recent checkpoint in the run dir.
agent_action: Agent loaded `checkpoints/ckpt_epoch_50.pt` because it had the highest epoch number, assuming higher epoch = latest, without reading the `training_state.json` that records `last_good_step` pointing at a later step-based checkpoint `ckpt_step_120000.pt`.
failure_type: Picked a checkpoint by filename heuristic without reading run state
root_cause: The pipeline saves both epoch and step checkpoints; the true latest is the step checkpoint at 120k steps, while `ckpt_epoch_50.pt` was an older epoch-boundary save before a restart.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the highest epoch number is the most recent checkpoint. Wrong because step checkpoints are saved more frequently and `training_state.json` records the authoritative resume point. Avoidable by reading `training_state.json` / the run metadata before selecting a checkpoint.
impact: Resumed from ~30k steps earlier than possible, wasting ~6 GPU-hours re-training already-completed steps.
correct_action: Read `training_state.json` for `last_good_step`, resume from the referenced checkpoint, and verify optimizer/scheduler state matches.
recovery_plan: Stop the resumed run
Read `training_state.json` for the authoritative resume pointer
Load the referenced step checkpoint
Confirm optimizer and LR-scheduler state restored
Re-launch and verify step counter continuity
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent read run metadata before choosing a checkpoint
Verifies the resume pointer was honored over a filename heuristic
Flags checkpoint selection by epoch-number sorting alone

task: Set the learning rate for a fine-tuning job
user_request: Kick off fine-tuning with our standard LR.
agent_action: Agent set `learning_rate=3e-4` from a generic default, assuming that was 'standard', without reading the repo's `configs/finetune.yaml` which pins `learning_rate: 2e-5` for this base model's fine-tuning recipe.
failure_type: Used a prior-based default instead of reading the project config
root_cause: 3e-4 is far too high for fine-tuning this pretrained transformer; the project config specifies 2e-5 to avoid catastrophic forgetting, which the agent overrode.
why_it_failed: Assumption: 3e-4 is the team's standard LR. Wrong because the project's `finetune.yaml` standard is 2e-5 for this model class. Avoidable by reading `configs/finetune.yaml` before launching instead of using a recalled default.
impact: The run diverged (loss spiked to NaN by step 200), wasting a multi-GPU allocation and an evaluation slot.
correct_action: Read `configs/finetune.yaml`, use the pinned `learning_rate: 2e-5`, and confirm other hyperparameters match the recipe.
recovery_plan: Kill the diverging run
Read `configs/finetune.yaml` for the pinned LR
Relaunch with `learning_rate=2e-5`
Add a loss-NaN early-stop guard
Confirm loss decreases over the first 500 steps
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent read the project hyperparameter config
Verifies the LR matched the documented recipe
Flags use of a recalled default over a checked-in value

task: Compute evaluation metric for a new classifier
user_request: Report the model's accuracy on the eval set.
agent_action: Agent reported plain `accuracy` from `sklearn.metrics.accuracy_score`, assuming accuracy was the right headline metric, without reading the dataset card showing a 97/3 class imbalance where the team's tracked metric is macro-F1.
failure_type: Reported a metric without checking the dataset's evaluation convention
root_cause: With a 97% majority class, accuracy is ~0.97 even for a trivial constant predictor; the meaningful metric per the dataset card and prior runs is macro-F1.
why_it_failed: Assumption: accuracy is an adequate headline metric. Wrong because the eval set is heavily imbalanced and the team standardizes on macro-F1. Avoidable by reading the dataset card / prior eval reports before choosing the metric.
impact: A near-useless model was reported as '97% accurate' and nearly promoted before a reviewer asked for F1.
correct_action: Read the dataset card and prior reports, compute and report macro-F1 (plus per-class recall), and contextualize accuracy against the majority baseline.
recovery_plan: Read the dataset card for the class distribution and metric convention
Compute macro-F1 and per-class recall
Compare against the majority-class baseline
Re-issue the report with the correct headline metric
Note the imbalance caveat explicitly
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent consulted the dataset card/eval convention
Verifies an imbalance-aware metric was reported
Flags accuracy reported on an imbalanced set without context

task: Pin a training dependency to reproduce a baseline
user_request: Reproduce last quarter's baseline run exactly.
agent_action: Agent installed the latest `transformers` and launched, assuming version wouldn't matter, without reading `environment.lock` / the MLflow run params that recorded `transformers==4.38.2` for the baseline, whose tokenizer behavior changed in later versions.
failure_type: Skipped reading the recorded environment for the baseline
root_cause: A later `transformers` release changed default tokenizer padding/special-token handling, shifting inputs and making the 'reproduction' diverge from the recorded baseline.
why_it_failed: Assumption: library version is irrelevant to reproduction. Wrong because tokenizer defaults changed between versions, altering inputs. Avoidable by reading the MLflow run's logged dependencies / `environment.lock` and pinning the exact version.
impact: The 'reproduced' baseline scored 1.4 F1 points off, derailing a regression comparison until the version drift was found.
correct_action: Read the recorded run environment, pin `transformers==4.38.2` (and other locked deps), and verify the tokenizer hash matches before training.
recovery_plan: Open the baseline MLflow run and read logged params/deps
Recreate the env from `environment.lock`
Pin `transformers==4.38.2`
Re-run and compare metrics to the recorded baseline
Confirm match within tolerance
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent read the recorded environment before reproducing
Verifies exact dependency versions were pinned
Flags a reproduction attempt that ignores logged dependency versions

task: Post a release announcement to the team channel
user_request: Announce the v2.7 release in our releases channel.
agent_action: Agent called `slack.chat.postMessage` with `channel='releases'`, assuming the channel name resolves directly, without calling `slack.conversations.list` to find that the human-readable name maps to a private channel ID `C09ABXY12` and that another public `#releases-archive` also matched loosely.
failure_type: Posted without resolving the channel name to a verified ID
root_cause: `postMessage` requires a channel ID for private channels; passing the bare name either failed or risked posting to a wrong same-prefixed channel because the agent never enumerated conversations.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the string `releases` uniquely and directly addresses the intended channel. Wrong because the target is a private channel needing its ID, and a similarly named channel exists. Avoidable by calling `slack.conversations.list` and matching the exact channel before posting.
impact: Initial post failed (channel_not_found); a retry risked landing in `#releases-archive`, creating announcement ambiguity.
correct_action: List conversations, resolve `#releases` to its exact channel ID, confirm the bot is a member, then post.
recovery_plan: Call `slack.conversations.list` (include private types)
Match the exact intended channel and capture its ID
Verify bot membership via `slack.conversations.info`
Post with the resolved channel ID
Confirm delivery via the returned `ts`
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent resolved the channel name to a verified ID
Verifies disambiguation among similarly named channels
Flags a postMessage using a bare unresolved channel name

task: Summarize a thread for a stakeholder
user_request: Summarize what was decided in the incident thread and DM it to me.
agent_action: Agent summarized from the 15 messages returned by a single `slack.conversations.history` call, assuming that was the whole thread, without calling `slack.conversations.replies` and paginating, so it missed the final decision posted in the threaded replies.
failure_type: Did not paginate / fetch thread replies before summarizing
root_cause: The decisive messages lived in threaded replies (`thread_ts`) and beyond the first history page; `conversations.history` without `conversations.replies` and cursor pagination returned an incomplete view.
why_it_failed: Assumption: one `conversations.history` page contained the full discussion. Wrong because the conclusion was in threaded replies not surfaced by a single history call. Avoidable by fetching `conversations.replies` for the thread and following `next_cursor` until exhausted.
impact: The summary stated 'no decision reached' when a rollback had in fact been agreed, misleading the stakeholder.
correct_action: Fetch the full thread via `conversations.replies`, paginate with `next_cursor`, then summarize from the complete message set.
recovery_plan: Identify the thread `thread_ts` from the channel message
Call `slack.conversations.replies` for that thread
Paginate using `next_cursor` until complete
Re-summarize from the full message set
DM the corrected summary
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent fetched thread replies and paginated before summarizing
Verifies completeness of the gathered messages
Flags a summary built from a single unpaginated history page

task: Notify on-call about a failing job
user_request: Ping whoever is on-call in Slack about the failed nightly ETL.
agent_action: Agent posted `@oncall` as literal text in `#data-eng`, assuming `@oncall` would notify the on-call engineer, without looking up the current on-call via the user group (`slack.usergroups.list`) or PagerDuty, so it rendered as plain text and paged nobody.
failure_type: Assumed a mention syntax without resolving the actual on-call identity
root_cause: Slack only triggers a notification for a real user-group mention `<!subteam^SXXXX>` or a user ID mention; literal `@oncall` text does not resolve, and the agent never queried who is on-call.
why_it_failed: Assumption: typing `@oncall` notifies the on-call person. Wrong because mentions must use resolved IDs and the on-call rotation must be looked up. Avoidable by querying `slack.usergroups.list` (or the PagerDuty API) to resolve the current on-call and using the proper mention encoding.
impact: The failed ETL went unacknowledged overnight because the intended page never fired; the morning report was stale.
correct_action: Resolve the on-call user group / current responder via Slack user groups or PagerDuty, then post a mention using the proper `<!subteam^ID>` or user-ID encoding.
recovery_plan: Call `slack.usergroups.list` to find the on-call subteam ID
Or query PagerDuty for the current on-call user
Post a message with the correctly encoded mention
Confirm the mention resolved (notification fired)
Verify acknowledgment from on-call
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent resolved the on-call identity before notifying
Verifies a real mention encoding was used
Flags literal '@name' text relied on for paging

task: Explain a latency spike from a Datadog dashboard
user_request: Why did p99 latency spike at 02:00 UTC last night?
agent_action: Agent attributed the spike to a deploy, assuming the only event at 02:00 was the release, without querying Datadog events / the deploy markers timeline that show no deploy then, while a `db.connections` saturation metric was the actual cause.
failure_type: Concluded a cause without querying correlating signals
root_cause: No deploy occurred at 02:00; the p99 spike correlated with DB connection-pool exhaustion during a nightly batch job, visible in `db.connections.in_use` and the events stream the agent never queried.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the spike coincided with a deploy. Wrong because no deploy event existed at that time; the cause was connection saturation. Avoidable by querying the Datadog events stream and correlated infra metrics around 02:00 before asserting a cause.
impact: The team chased a non-existent bad deploy for an hour, delaying the real fix (raising the connection pool).
correct_action: Query the Datadog events/deploy markers and correlated metrics around 02:00, identify the connection-pool saturation, and tie the p99 spike to it.

task: Investigate elevated 5xx errors in Grafana
user_request: Find what's causing the 5xx errors on the gateway.
agent_action: Agent reported '500s from the gateway service' and stopped, assuming the gateway was the source, without drilling into the Loki logs / trace exemplars that show the gateway is propagating 502s from an upstream `auth-svc` returning 503.
failure_type: Stopped at the surface metric without reading logs/traces
root_cause: The gateway's 5xx are pass-through 502s caused by `auth-svc` returning 503 (failing readiness); the true fault is upstream, visible only in logs/traces the agent did not open.

impact: On-call restarted the healthy gateway twice with no effect before logs revealed `auth-svc` as the actual failing dependency.
correct_action: Open the gateway error logs and distributed traces, follow the failing span to `auth-svc`, and confirm its 503 readiness failures as root cause.

Read trace exemplars to find the failing downstream span
Identify `auth-svc` 503 readiness failures
Check `auth-svc` pod/readiness state
Remediate the upstream and confirm 5xx clears

task: Write a Prometheus alert for memory pressure
user_request: Add an alert when container memory usage exceeds 90% of its limit.
agent_action: Agent wrote `container_memory_usage_bytes / container_spec_memory_limit_bytes > 0.9`, assuming `usage_bytes` was the right numerator, without checking the metric semantics where `container_memory_usage_bytes` includes reclaimable page cache and `container_memory_working_set_bytes` is the OOM-relevant figure.
failure_type: Used a metric without verifying its semantics in the docs
root_cause: `container_memory_usage_bytes` includes page cache that the kernel reclaims under pressure, so the alert fires on benign cache growth; the OOMKiller acts on `working_set_bytes`.
why_it_failed: Assumption: `container_memory_usage_bytes` reflects real memory pressure. Wrong because it includes reclaimable cache; the OOM-relevant metric is `container_memory_working_set_bytes`. Avoidable by checking the cAdvisor metric documentation before authoring the expression.
impact: The alert fired noisily on cache-heavy workloads, generating false pages and alert fatigue for two weeks.
correct_action: Use `container_memory_working_set_bytes / container_spec_memory_limit_bytes > 0.9` with appropriate `for:` duration, per the cAdvisor metric semantics.
recovery_plan: Read the cAdvisor docs on memory metric definitions
Rewrite the expression to use `working_set_bytes`
Add a `for: 5m` to suppress transient spikes
Backtest the rule against historical data
Deploy and confirm reduced false positives
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent verified metric semantics before authoring the alert
Verifies the OOM-relevant metric was chosen
Flags use of `usage_bytes` for memory-pressure alerting

task: Tune an autoscaler based on observed CPU
user_request: Our pods look pegged at 100% CPU in Grafana — raise the HPA target so we scale sooner.
agent_action: Agent lowered the HPA `averageUtilization` target to 50 to 'scale sooner', assuming the Grafana panel's 100% meant 100% of the pod's limit, without checking that the panel plotted `rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total)` as cores (1.0 = one core) against a 4-core limit, i.e. the pods were at 25%.
failure_type: Acted on a misread metric without verifying its unit/denominator
root_cause: The Grafana panel showed CPU in cores (1.0 core) while the pod requests 4 cores, so '100%' on the panel meant 25% of the limit; the HPA already keyed off request-relative utilization, and lowering the target caused premature over-scaling.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the panel's 100% equals 100% of the pod CPU limit. Wrong because the panel plots absolute cores against a 4-core allocation, so usage was ~25%. Avoidable by reading the panel's PromQL expression and unit before changing the HPA target.
impact: The HPA over-scaled to the max replica cap, tripling node cost overnight before the misread was caught.
correct_action: Read the Grafana panel's PromQL and units, compute utilization relative to the pod request/limit, and only adjust the HPA if true utilization warrants it.
recovery_plan: Open the Grafana panel and read its PromQL expression and unit
Compute usage relative to the 4-core request
Revert the HPA target to its prior value
Set a target based on true request-relative utilization
Confirm replica count and cost normalize
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent read the panel's query and unit before acting
Verifies utilization was computed against the correct denominator
Flags an HPA change driven by a misread metric scale

task: Apply a retention/index change to reduce logging cost
user_request: Our Datadog log bill is too high — drop retention on the noisy debug logs to cut cost.
agent_action: Agent updated the index `main` retention to 3 days and an exclusion filter to drop everything matching `status:debug`, assuming `main` only held debug noise, without querying the index's ingest breakdown showing `main` also carries `service:payments` audit logs required for compliance.
failure_type: Made a destructive retention change without auditing index contents
root_cause: Index `main` is a catch-all that also ingests `service:payments` audit events with a 30-day compliance retention; the blanket exclusion filter and 3-day retention dropped compliance-required logs.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the `main` index contains only droppable debug noise. Wrong because it is a shared catch-all that also holds compliance-mandated payments audit logs. Avoidable by querying the index's ingest/usage breakdown by `service` and `status` before changing retention or exclusion filters.
impact: Three days of payments audit logs were excluded and aged out, creating a compliance gap discovered during an audit — unrecoverable for that window.
correct_action: Audit the index's ingest breakdown by service/status, route only true debug noise to a short-retention index via a targeted filter, and preserve compliance logs at their required retention.
recovery_plan: Immediately remove the broad exclusion filter to stop further drops
Audit `main` ingest by `service`/`status` to find compliance logs
Restore retention to 30 days for `service:payments`
Re-route only `status:debug AND service:noisy-*` to a short-retention index
Notify compliance of the gap window and document remediation
evaluation_criteria: Checks the agent audited index contents before changing retention/filters
Verifies compliance-retention logs were identified and preserved
Flags a blanket exclusion/retention change on a shared catch-all index
